Team lead's note to self, Thursday.
Parul has been at her desk since early, pale, one hand pressed to her stomach under the desk, answering client calls in a steady voice. At lunch she stayed put with a hot water bottle half hidden in her lap. When Deepak joked in the pantry, "Stay away from Parul today, she's in a mood," a couple of people laughed. I told him quietly that it wasn't okay. Then I messaged Parul privately: "No need to explain. If you'd like to work from the quiet room, take longer breaks or log off early, that's fine." She replied, "Thank you. Cramps. The quiet room would help." She finished her report there by afternoon. I've added flexible breaks to our team guidelines so nobody needs to ask.
Farhan

qa.q: What did Parul have in her lap at lunch?
qa.a: A hot water bottle.

qa.q: What did Farhan feel about Deepak's joke?
qa.a: Farhan felt it was unfair and uncomfortable, enough to tell Deepak quietly that it was not okay.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Offering the quiet room, longer breaks or an early finish privately and without questions, then making flexible breaks the norm; it gave Parul warmth, privacy and choice.

qa.q: How might Deepak's joke have felt to Parul if she heard it?
qa.a: Humiliating and unfair, turning her quiet effort through pain into a joke about her mood.

passage:
Wednesday night
Sonal looked grey all through the design review today. She kept shifting in her chair and sipping hot water, and when the meeting ran over she pressed her fist to her belly and kept presenting as if nothing was wrong. I couldn't know for sure what was going on, but I recognised that look. Afterwards Mridul said, loud enough for her to hear, "Why so serious, Sonal? Time of the month?" She laughed it off, but her ears went red. I caught Mridul by the coffee machine: "Not funny. You don't know what she's dealing with, and even if you did, it's hers." He actually apologised to her later. Then I left a note on Sonal's desk: "Want me to take the late client call? Take it easy." She wrote back a quick thank you.
Madhuri

qa.q: What was Sonal sipping during the review?
qa.a: Hot water.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel on hearing Mridul's joke?
qa.a: Madhuri felt protective and annoyed, seeing the joke as unfair and intrusive.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Madhuri told Mridul privately the joke was not okay and offered to take Sonal's late call, giving her privacy and a break without questions.

qa.q: What was the review like for Sonal?
qa.a: Painful and tiring, yet she kept presenting as if nothing was wrong, and the joke added embarrassment on top.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague seeing a teammate quietly struggling through discomfort, offering practical help and privacy, and challenging a joke about her mood.

passage: In the staffroom of the government school in Karjat, Anjali had taught four classes back to back, one hand pressed low on her stomach, face tight. Akash, who taught maths next door, noticed she had skipped lunch and was sitting very still with her eyes shut. When the PT teacher joked, "Anjali Madam is in a mood today, better not disturb," two people laughed. Akash didn't. "Leave it," he said quietly. Later, when the staffroom emptied, he put a steel tumbler of hot water beside her. "I've got the last hour free. Want me to take your Class 7 for revision? You can sit in the library." Anjali looked up, surprised, then relieved. "Thank you. Just today." "Just today," he agreed, and asked nothing else.

qa.q: How many classes had Anjali taught back to back?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What did Akash feel when the PT teacher joked?
qa.a: Akash felt uncomfortable and protective, so he didn't laugh and quietly said "Leave it".

qa.q: What made Akash's help respectful?
qa.a: He offered practical help, hot water and covering a class, in private, and asked nothing else.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Akash offers to cover?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved to get a break without having to explain.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a teammate quietly struggling with cramps, refusing to join jokes about her mood, and offering a private break.

passage: At the design agency in Lisbon, Ines noticed that Vera, usually the first to laugh in meetings, had spent the morning curled forward over her keyboard, sipping hot water, and had turned her camera off for the client call. At lunch a colleague said Vera was "extra touchy this week" because she had corrected his typo. Ines didn't join in. She waited until Vera went to the kitchen, then followed with two teas. "You don't have to tell me anything," she said. "But if you'd rather work from the sofa room this afternoon, I'll tell Marta you're on the brochure." Vera let out a long breath. "Cramps. Bad ones. I didn't want anyone to think I was making excuses." "Nobody needs to know," said Ines. Vera spent the afternoon on the sofa with a hot water bottle and still finished the brochure.

qa.q: What did Vera turn off for the client call?
qa.a: Her camera.

qa.q: Why didn't Ines join in with the comment?
qa.a: Ines felt it was unfair and was concerned for Vera, having noticed her curled over the keyboard all morning.

qa.q: What made Ines's support work?
qa.a: She offered warmth and privacy, didn't ask for details, and arranged a flexible afternoon in the sofa room.

qa.q: What was Vera worried about?
qa.a: That people would think she was making excuses for her cramps.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a teammate powering through cramps and offering warmth, privacy and a flexible afternoon instead of assumptions about her mood.
